strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel direction: applying mechanistic interpretability (MLP value-vector probing à la Geva et al.) to preference prediction rather than binary factual correctness, extending the 'hidden knowledge' line of work (Gekhman et al., 2025; Orgad et al., 2025) to inherently distributional, contextual outcomes.

The empirical scale is impressive and well beyond comparable persona-simulation studies: 7 model families (base and instruction-tuned), 6 national elections from representative surveys, 280,000 persona combinations, 10 hand-crafted and native-speaker-verified prompt templates per country, and over 24 million configurations.

The methodological pipeline is carefully validated: label-shuffled and random-weight controls, regression baselines, sign-inversion (local necessity) tests, a non-political intervention control (Figure 9), an in-context learning baseline that controls for the external party-position data (Figure 10), and a layer-window ablation (Figure 7). This is more rigorous than typical probing papers.

The framing of findings is honest and appropriately hedged: the authors consistently report that gains are 'selective rather than uniform,' distinguish demographic from opinion-based attributes, and derive an interpretable entropy-gating criterion for when latent estimation helps.

Reproducibility is strong: probe datasets, prompt templates, and code are released; the limitations and impact statements are thoughtful and candid (first-order approximation, white-box requirement, misuse risks).
weaknesses: The headline win-rate results (Figures 2, 4) are presented descriptively without confidence intervals or formal significance tests on whether latent estimation systematically outperforms probability-based estimation. Figure 11 shows Δk distributions straddling zero for most model-country pairs, so the aggregate claim that mechanistic forecasting 'improves prediction accuracy' rests on win-rate proportions whose uncertainty is not quantified.

Probe F1 scores exceeding 96% are suspiciously high and raise the concern that probes capture superficial, token-level party markers (e.g., party names in the shuffled-party-list) rather than deep party structure; near-perfect generalization from voting-advice statements to persona prompts would be remarkable and warrants more scrutiny of potential leakage from the probe prompt templates.

The effect sizes are modest and the practical significance is not fully established: the paper never evaluates against actual election outcomes, only against (weighted) survey distributions, and the median absolute errors in Figures 3 and 5 remain large (often 10-30 percentage points), so neither method produces usable forecasts in an absolute sense.

The entropy-gating threshold of 0.85 appears post hoc and its selection is not justified or validated out-of-sample; the regression relating Δk to entropy is only described at a high level, and evaluating the gate only on cases with Δk > 0 risks circularity.

The probability-based baseline may be under-powered: it is pure next-token probability aggregation, whereas the latent method benefits from explicit calibration against party-position data; stronger surface-level baselines (e.g., logit ensembling, prompt ensembling with the same party-position data) are only partially covered by the ICL baseline.

Some presentation issues reduce clarity: several figures (e.g., Figures 2 and 5) have illegible axis labels and dense layouts; key quantitative details (probe dimensions, number of selected value vectors per party, normalization details in Eq. 13) are relegated or unspecified in the main text.
